questions.q: What changes about the risk of a prompt injection attack once an LLM is wired up with tool use or function calling, turning it into an agent?
options: A successful injection can now produce a real-world action — sending an email, issuing a refund, writing to a repository — not just a bad text response
Nothing changes; chat-only models and tool-using agents have identical risk profiles
Tool-using agents become immune to prompt injection because tool calls are always validated by the cloud provider
The risk decreases, because tool use requires additional authentication that blocks all injected instructions
questions.explain: A chatbot's failure mode is bounded to bad text. An agent with tool access converts a successful injection into an actual action with real-world consequences.

questions.q: How does this lesson define the question to ask about every tool wired up to an LLM agent?
options: Would this tool be useful to have available someday
Does this specific task strictly require this capability, or does granting it create blast radius with no benefit to the legitimate use case
Does this tool increase the number of API calls the vendor can bill for
Would removing this tool make the demo look less impressive
questions.explain: Least privilege applied to agents means granting only what the specific task strictly requires — every extra permission is pure downside risk that an injection attack can exploit for free.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of read/write separation as described in this lesson?
options: Giving the agent one bundled service account with full mailbox access
Removing all logging so the agent's actions cannot be reconstructed later
An agent that reads a mailbox to summarize it holding a different, lower trust tier than one that can also send or delete messages
Letting the agent send and delete emails without any additional gate once it can read them
questions.explain: Read access and write/send/delete access should sit on separate, deliberately-granted tools rather than one combined permission, so reading doesn't imply the ability to act.

questions.q: What does this lesson identify as the same pattern as human-in-the-loop approval for consequential LLM agent actions?
options: The approval-gate design used for high-risk SOAR playbook actions, where an automated response pauses for an analyst's sign-off instead of firing unattended
A CAPTCHA presented to the end user before every chat message
A firewall rule that blocks all outbound traffic from the agent's host
A password rotation policy applied to the agent's service account
questions.explain: This lesson explicitly ties the agent approval-gate pattern back to the same human-sign-off design already covered for high-risk SOAR automation earlier in this path.

questions.q: Why does this lesson call privilege separation the most durable control in the chapter, compared to input filtering?
options: It requires no implementation effort and works automatically out of the box
It only applies to agents built by large, well-funded companies
It replaces the need for any logging or monitoring

It doesn't need to anticipate every possible attacker phrasing — the agent physically cannot perform an action it was never granted the capability to perform, regardless of how clever the injected instruction is
questions.explain: Input filtering has to guess every possible phrasing an attacker might try. Privilege separation bounds the consequence of an attack instead, so it holds up even against phrasing nobody has seen before.
